faults.evidence: Arrian 1.7: "and on the seventh day arrived at Pelina in Thessaly. Starting thence, he entered Boeotia on the sixth day" (.references/archive.org-download-theanabasisofale46976gut-46976-0.txt.txt, line 1239). Bosworth reads the same count as "On the seventh day's march he had reached Pelinna ... Five days later he entered Boeotia" (.references/archive.org-onquest-20and-20Empire-20The-20Reign-20of-20Alexander-20the-20Great-20-281993-29-djvu.txt.txt, line 1415). Arrian counts inclusively and gives no "six days later"; with the body fixed, the note's "Bosworth counts five days" reads as a gloss on the same count and not as a second account.
faults.action: Leaving Pelinna, he enters Boeotia on the sixth day, by Arrian's count.\*

faults.evidence: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire, ch. 2.I: "The new king could not leave Macedonia to deal with Greek unrest, still less fight an extended campaign in the north, if there were still unsatisfied contenders for power at home." (.references/archive.org-onquest-20and-20Empire-20The-20Reign-20of-20Alexander-20the-20Great-20-281993-29-djvu.txt.txt, line 1275). The sentence keeps Bosworth's words and the order of his clauses outside quotation marks.
faults.action: As long as a rival for the throne lived, Bosworth argues, Alexander could not safely march out of Macedon, south to Greece or north to the tribes.

faults.evidence: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire, ch. 2.II: "The only military action was at the very beginning, when the Thessalians attempted to block the main route through the vale of Tempe. The young king promptly circumvented their position, driving south along the coast and cutting steps in the face of Mt Ossa to bring his army into Thessaly to the rear of the enemy. That was the end of armed resistance." (.references/archive.org-onquest-20and-20Empire-20The-20Reign-20of-20Alexander-20the-20Great-20-281993-29-djvu.txt.txt, lines 1285-1288). The two sentences follow Bosworth's wording and clause order.
faults.action: The Thessalians bar his way at the vale of Tempe. He turns them by the shore, where his men hew footholds into the side of Mount Ossa, and the army comes down into Thessaly at their back. It is the only fighting of the march.

faults.evidence: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire, ch. 2.II: "The pass actually taken was probably the Trojan, on the later Roman road between Philippopolis and Oescus, but the more easterly Shipka pass cannot be ruled out." (.references/archive.org-onquest-20and-20Empire-20The-20Reign-20of-20Alexander-20the-20Great-20-281993-29-djvu.txt.txt, line 1310); Bosworth, Commentary on 1.1.5: "who opts for the Shipka pass, the favourite of modern scholars" (.references/archive.org-History-20of-20Alexander-3B-20Volume-20I-20Books-20I-III-20-20A.-20B.-20Bosworth-djvu.txt.txt, line 4051); Hammond: "He led his army up to a central pass (probably the Shipka pass)" (.references/archive.org-20Griffith-20G.-20A-20history-20of-20Macedonia.-20V.3-2C-20336-167-20B.C.-201988-djvu.txt.txt, line 4433), in "PART ONE (by N. G. L. HAMMOND)" (same file, lines 615-618). The note keeps Bosworth's wording in both sentences, and "the favourite of earlier scholars" is Bosworth's phrase, not Hammond's; part one of the History of Macedonia III is Hammond's alone.
faults.action: Bosworth favours the Trojan pass, which the Romans later used for their road from Philippopolis to the Danube, but leaves the Shipka pass open. Hammond favours the Shipka, as most scholars before Bosworth had.
